lesson.title: Shifting the Curve: Directional Selection in Action
lesson.summary: Directional selection favors one extreme of a trait's distribution over the other, steadily shifting the population's average in that direction across generations, the pattern behind the evolution of antibiotic resistance.
lesson.body:
Directional selection is the pattern in which individuals at one end of a trait's distribution consistently have higher relative fitness than the population average, while individuals at the opposite end have lower fitness. Unlike stabilizing selection, which trims both tails and holds the average steady, directional selection pushes the entire distribution toward one extreme over successive generations. This is the pattern most people picture when they think of natural selection in action, because it produces the kind of visible, directional change, a population looking measurably different after enough generations, that is easiest to observe and document.

Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is a clear, well documented example. Within any bacterial population there is typically some natural variation in resistance to a given antibiotic, often due to differences at one or a few genes, some already present before the antibiotic is ever introduced. When that antibiotic is applied, bacteria with lower resistance die at much higher rates, while the small fraction with higher resistance survive and reproduce, passing their resistance alleles on to all of their offspring. Each subsequent generation starts from a population enriched for resistance alleles, so continued exposure to the antibiotic keeps favoring the same end of the distribution. Over relatively few generations, which for fast reproducing bacteria can mean days to weeks, the population's average resistance level shifts substantially upward, exactly the signature of directional selection: one extreme of the original distribution becoming the new normal.

At the level of allele frequency, directional selection is the pattern most likely to drive an allele all the way to fixation, because the same allele is favored generation after generation rather than being favored only when paired with a particular partner allele. This is also why directional selection shows up so reliably whenever an environment changes in a consistent, sustained way, whether that is a new selective pressure like an antibiotic, a shifting climate, or a new predator, because a consistent new pressure means one end of a trait's existing variation suddenly has a relative fitness advantage it did not have before. As long as that pressure continues and heritable variation for the trait exists, directional selection keeps shifting the population, generation after generation, toward whichever extreme now confers the higher fitness.
